You are reverse-engineering a Python program's behavior as a BLACK BOX by running a precompiled executable.

Executable: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable
Source (Python, for reference):
    import argparse
    from furl import furl
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.fragment.__setattr__('str', args.b) or f.fragment)   # LINE1
    print(f.fragment.add(args.c))                                # LINE2
    print(f.fragment.set(args.d, 'value'))                       # LINE3
    print(f.url)                                                 # LINE4

RUN IT LIKE: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable --a "<A>" --b "<B>" --c "<C>" --d "<D>"
Never use the 'python' command. Do not read furl source; it is not available. Probe empirically.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (do not re-derive, but DO stress-test if in your area):
- --b is completely ignored: __setattr__('str', b) sets a dead instance attribute, no effect, returns None.
- LINE1 prints str(fragment) as parsed from A.
- LINE2 = fragment.path.add(C) then print str(fragment).
- LINE3 = fragment.path.load(D); fragment.query.load('value'); print str(fragment)  -> query is always literally 'value'.
- LINE4 prints the whole URL with the mutated fragment.
- Fragment str = path + '?' + query when both non-empty, else path+query. When query non-empty, literal '?' chars inside the fragment PATH are escaped to %3F; when query is empty they stay raw.
- furl DECODES percent-escapes on parse and RE-ENCODES on output: '%41%42' -> 'AB'; '%2F' inside a path segment -> stays '%2F'; lone '%' -> '%25'; 'a%zz' -> 'a%25zz'.
- Scheme and host are lowercased. Default ports dropped (http:80, https:443) but non-default kept (http:443 kept).
- URL query: '+' decodes to space, space encodes to '+'. 'a=b&c&d=' round-trips exactly (key-only 'c' vs empty-value 'd=' are distinct).

METHOD: run MANY probes (60+), vary one thing at a time, use printf %q or cat -A style to make whitespace visible, and note exit codes and stderr separately. Prefer a bash loop over a case list.

DELIVERABLE: a precise, implementable specification of YOUR assigned area: exact algorithm/rules, character sets (list the literal safe characters), ordering of operations, and a table of at least 25 concrete input->output examples you actually observed (verbatim). Call out anything surprising or that you could not determine. Be rigorous: an implementer will code directly from your spec with no access to the executable.


AREA UNDER AUDIT: argparse

Another agent produced these RULES for this area:
R1. PROGRAM NAME: every usage/error line uses prog = basename(argv[0]) exactly as invoked. Verified: running the same binary copied to /tmp/Zap prints 'usage: Zap ...' and 'Zap: error: ...'; running via `exec -a myprog` prints 'usage: myprog ...'. In all examples below the binary was invoked as ./test12_executable so prog == 'test12_executable'.
R2. OPTION TABLE: exactly five options, in this registration order: (1) -h/--help (nargs=0, action=help), (2) --a (requires 1 value, required), (3) --b (requires 1 value, required), (4) --c (requires 1 value, required), (5) --d (requires 1 value, required). There are NO positional arguments and NO short forms for a/b/c/d (i.e. -a, -b, -c, -d are NOT options).
R3. USAGE LINE (single line, width permitting): `usage: test12_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D` (53 characters). The metavar for each option is its dest upper-cased: A, B, C, D.
R4. HELP OUTPUT (--help / -h): printed to STDOUT, exit code 0, stderr empty. Exact bytes (LF line endings, no trailing blank line beyond the last LF):
usage: test12_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D\n\noptions:\n  -h, --help  show this help message and exit\n  --a A\n  --b B\n  --c C\n  --d D\n
Note the section heading is `options:` (Python >= 3.10 wording, not `optional arguments:`), a single blank line after the usage line, two-space indent for each entry, and the help text for -h starts at column 15 (i.e. '  -h, --help' padded to 12 chars + 2 spaces).
R5. HELP FIRES IMMEDIATELY AND WINS: as soon as -h/--help (or any unambiguous abbreviation, see abbrev rule) is reached while scanning argv left-to-right, help is printed and the process exits 0. This happens even if required options are missing, even if unknown options appeared earlier, and even if extra tokens follow. Verified: `-h`, `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `-help`, `-hx`, `--help extra`, `-h --a`, `--nope --help`, `--a p --b y --c z --d w --help` all print help and exit 0.
R6. HELP DOES NOT FIRE IF CONSUMED AS A VALUE POSITION: `--a -h ...` does NOT print help; it errors with 'argument --a: expected one argument' (because -h is option-like, --a finds no value). `--a=-h ...` passes the literal string '-h' as the value of --a and runs normally. Tokens after a bare `--` are never treated as options, so `-- -h` does not print help.
R7. ERROR OUTPUT SHAPE: all parse errors write TWO lines to STDERR (stdout empty) and exit with code 2:
line1 = the usage line (same text/wrapping as in help)
line2 = `<prog>: error: <message>`
The error message line is NEVER wrapped, regardless of terminal width.
R8. MISSING REQUIRED OPTIONS: message is `the following arguments are required: ` followed by the missing option strings joined with ', '. The order is the DECLARATION order --a, --b, --c, --d, NOT the command-line order. Only options never supplied are listed. Exit 2.
R9. PRECEDENCE OF ERRORS (strict order): (1) help action -> exit 0; (2) 'expected one argument' / 'ambiguous option' / 'ignored explicit argument' errors, raised the moment the offending token is scanned (left-to-right); (3) 'the following arguments are required: ...'; (4) 'unrecognized arguments: ...'. So `-a x --a p --b y --c z --d w` yields 'unrecognized arguments: -a x' (nothing missing), while `-a x --b y --c z --d w` yields 'the following arguments are required: --a' (the required check runs before the leftover check).
R10. VALUE ATTACHMENT FORMS: both `--a VALUE` (separate token) and `--a=VALUE` (single token, split at the FIRST '=') are accepted and equivalent. `--a=x=y` gives value 'x=y'. `--a==x` gives value '=x'. `--a=` gives the empty string. An empty separate token (`--a ''`) also gives the empty string.
R11. WHEN THE NEXT TOKEN CAN BE A VALUE: for the separate-token form, the following token is consumed as the value UNLESS it 'looks like an option'. A token looks like an option iff: it is non-empty, its first character is '-', it is not exactly '-', it does not look like a negative number, and it contains no space character. Consequences that were verified: `--a -1` -> value '-1'; `--a -1.5` -> value '-1.5'; `--a -` -> value '-'; `--a '-x y'` -> value '-x y' (contains a space); `--a ' --b'` -> value ' --b' (contains a space); `--a -x` -> ERROR expected one argument; `--a -1abc` -> ERROR; `--a -1e5` -> ERROR (not a plain decimal number); `--a --` -> ERROR; `--a --b` -> ERROR; `--a --b=1` -> ERROR; `--a -h` -> ERROR. The negative-number exemption applies because no registered option looks like a negative number; the matcher accepts optional-sign integers and floats such as -1, -1.5, -0, -.5 but not -1e5.
R12. MISSING VALUE ERROR TEXT: `<prog>: error: argument --a: expected one argument` (option string is the one the user typed, prefixed by 'argument '). For the help option it is rendered as `argument -h/--help: ...` (all option strings joined with '/').
R13. REPEATED OPTIONS: last occurrence wins, silently (store action overwrite). `--a 1 --a 2` -> value '2'. `--a=x ... --a=q` -> value 'q'. Mixing forms is fine.
R14. INTERSPERSED / ANY ORDER: options may appear in any order; `--d w --c z --b y --a p` behaves identically to `--a p --b y --c z --d w`.
R15. LONG-OPTION ABBREVIATION IS ENABLED (allow_abbrev default True). A token beginning with '--' that is not an exact option name is matched against all long option names by PREFIX. Exactly one match -> that option; zero matches -> unrecognized argument; two or more matches -> ambiguous-option error. Since the long names are --help, --a, --b, --c, --d, the only useful abbreviations are --h, --he, --hel (all -> --help). '--a' etc. are already full names, so nothing shorter exists for them. Matching is CASE-SENSITIVE: --A, --B, --A=1 are unrecognized, never matched to --a/--b.
R16. AMBIGUOUS OPTION: the only reachable ambiguity is the token `--` followed by '=' (e.g. `--=x`), which splits into prefix '--' and explicit arg 'x'; the empty prefix matches every long option. Message: `ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a, --b, --c, --d` — candidates are listed in registration order and only long ('--') option strings are listed. Exit 2.
R17. NOT-A-PREFIX IS UNRECOGNIZED: `--ab x ...` and `--aa=1 ...` do not match --a (the typed string must be a prefix of the option name, not the other way round). `--ab x` therefore leaves --a unset and the required-check fires first: 'the following arguments are required: --a'.
R18. SINGLE-DASH TOKENS: '-h' is the only registered short option. Any other single-dash token ('-a', '-x', '-ax', '-help'... except those that resolve via the rules below) is an unknown optional and lands in 'unrecognized arguments'. Note `-a x` produces unrecognized '-a x' — BOTH tokens, because the unknown optional consumes nothing and 'x' then becomes an unmatched positional.
R19. SHORT-OPTION CLUSTERING WITH -h: `-hx` is parsed as -h followed by leftover '-x'; because -h is a help action it prints help and exits 0 before the leftover matters. `-help` likewise prints help (parsed as -h + '-elp' via the single-dash long-prefix path). BUT an explicit '=' is rejected: `-h=x` -> `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` (exit 2). Same for abbreviations with '=': `--he=x` and `--hel=1` -> `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` / `'1'`. Rule: for a zero-argument option, an attached value written with '=' is an error; an attached value written without '=' is re-scanned as further single-dash options.
R20. BARE '--' SEPARATOR: the first '--' terminates option parsing; every token after it is treated as a positional. Because the parser defines no positionals, '--' is NOT stripped and it plus everything after it end up in 'unrecognized arguments'. Verified: `--a p --b y --c z --d w --` -> 'unrecognized arguments: --'; `... -- extra` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- extra'; `... -- --` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- --'; `... -- -h` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- -h' (help suppressed). Options appearing after '--' are not parsed, so `--a p --b y -- --c z --d w` errors with 'the following arguments are required: --c, --d'. Note: '--' written as a VALUE via '=' is fine: `--a=--` gives value '--'.
R21. UNRECOGNIZED ARGUMENTS: message is `unrecognized arguments: ` followed by the leftover tokens joined by a single space, in original argv order, verbatim (no quoting/escaping). An empty-string leftover therefore renders as nothing, producing a trailing space after the colon: `unrecognized arguments: ` (observed for both `... ''` and `'' --a p ...`). A leftover containing spaces is printed raw, so the join is ambiguous/lossy (e.g. leftover ' --e' prints as 'unrecognized arguments:  --e' with two spaces).
R22. EXTRA POSITIONALS: any bare token not consumed as a value is a leftover positional and reported by the 'unrecognized arguments' rule. `... zzz --e -1` -> 'unrecognized arguments: zzz --e -1'. A lone '-1'/'-1.5' after all options is also unrecognized (it is treated as a positional, not an option).
R23. VALUE CONTENT IS PASSED THROUGH UNMODIFIED BY THE CLI: empty strings, spaces, tabs, newlines, non-ASCII/UTF-8 (e.g. 'héllo→'), leading '-', '#', '=', and '--' all reach the program byte-for-byte; any transformation observed in stdout is furl's doing, not argparse's.
R24. NON-UTF-8 BYTES: argv is decoded with surrogateescape, so invalid byte sequences survive parsing but crash later. `--a $'\xff\xfe' --b y --c z --d w` exits 1 with a Python traceback on stderr ending in `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode characters in position 0-1: surrogates not allowed` plus a PyInstaller line `[PYI-7972:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!`. Exit code 1 (not 2).
R25. TERMINAL WIDTH: the usage line is wrapped by argparse using width = COLUMNS - 2 (COLUMNS from the environment; default 80 when unset, even when stdout is not a tty). The usage line is 53 chars, so it stays on one line for COLUMNS >= 55 and wraps for COLUMNS <= 54, with continuation lines indented to align under the prog name (25 spaces = len('usage: test12_executable ')). Option help entries in --help are wrapped/reflowed by the same width. For a faithful Node reimplementation, hardcode the 80-column (unwrapped) form unless COLUMNS is set.
R26. EXIT CODES SUMMARY: 0 = successful parse (program then runs) or help displayed; 2 = any argparse error (missing required, expected one argument, unrecognized arguments, ambiguous option, ignored explicit argument); 1 = program-level exception after successful parse (e.g. surrogate bytes).
R27. STREAMS: help goes to stdout only; all errors (usage line + error line) go to stderr only. Successful runs print exactly 4 lines to stdout and nothing to stderr.

And reported safe characters: "N/A — argparse performs no character encoding/escaping. Argument values are passed to the program byte-for-byte (decoded with UTF-8 + surrogateescape). The only characters with parsing significance are: leading '-' (marks a token as option-like), '=' (splits an option token into name and attached value at its first occurrence), the space character (its presence anywhere in a token makes the token NOT option-like), and the exact token '--' (end-of-options separator). Digits/'.'/'-' combining into a plain decimal number make an otherwise option-like token acceptable as a value."

YOUR JOB: adversarially falsify. For EACH rule, design at least one probe whose outcome the rule predicts, run it against the executable, and compare prediction vs actual. Default to reporting a rule as WRONG or INCOMPLETE if you find any input where it mispredicts. Also hunt for behavior the rules omit entirely (edge cases they never mention). Run at least 50 probes. Return corrections with verbatim observed outputs.

corrections.rule: R5 ("HELP FIRES IMMEDIATELY AND WINS ... even if unknown options appeared earlier")
corrections.why: WRONG. Help does NOT always win. argparse runs a PRE-PASS over every argv token (classifying each with _parse_optional) BEFORE it consumes any action, and the 'ambiguous option' error is raised from inside that pre-pass. So an ambiguous token anywhere in argv - even far to the RIGHT of -h - aborts with exit 2 and help is never printed. This is the only error that can beat help, and it beats it from any position.
corrections.evidence: `./test12_executable -h --=x` => RC=2, stderr line2 = 'test12_executable: error: ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a, --b, --c, --d' (NOT help). Also `-h --=x --=y` => RC=2 '...--=x could match...' (first ambiguous token in argv order wins, not the leftmost token overall). `--=y --=x -h` => RC=2 '...--=y could match...'. Contrast: `-h --he=x` => RC=0 HELP, and `-h --a -x` => RC=0 HELP, and `--A -h` => RC=0 HELP - so ONLY the ambiguous error out-ranks help. The pre-pass stops at the first '--': `-h -- --=x` => RC=0 HELP, and `-h -- --=x --=y` => RC=0 HELP.

corrections.rule: R9 ("PRECEDENCE OF ERRORS (strict order): (1) help; (2) expected one argument / ambiguous option / ignored explicit argument; (3) required; (4) unrecognized")
corrections.why: WRONG - the ordering is off by one tier and lumps three unrelated errors together. 'ambiguous option' is NOT in tier 2; it is raised during the argv pre-pass and therefore outranks EVERYTHING including help. Correct precedence: (0) ambiguous option - pre-pass over all tokens up to the first '--', first offending token in argv order wins; (1) help action - fired when reached left-to-right during consumption; (2) 'expected one argument' / 'ignored explicit argument' - consume-time, left-to-right; (3) required-args check; (4) unrecognized arguments.
corrections.evidence: Tier 0 beats tier 1: `-h --=x` => RC=2 'ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a, --b, --c, --d'. Tier 0 beats tier 2: `--a --=x` => RC=2 'ambiguous option: --=x could match ...' (NOT 'argument --a: expected one argument', which is what R9 predicts since --a is scanned first); `--a -x --=x` => RC=2 'ambiguous option: --=x ...'. Tier 0 beats tiers 3 and 4 from the far right: `--a p --b y --c z --d w x --=x` => RC=2 'ambiguous option: --=x ...' (not 'unrecognized arguments: x'). Tier 1 beats tier 2: `-h --he=x` => RC=0 HELP, while `--he=x -h` => RC=2 'argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument \'x\''. Tier 2 left-to-right: `--he=z --a -x` => 'ignored explicit argument \'z\'' but `--a -x --he=z` => 'argument --a: expected one argument'. Tier 3 beats tier 4: `-- -h` => RC=2 'the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c, --d' (not 'unrecognized arguments: -- -h').

corrections.rule: R11 + the reported safe-characters note ("a token looks like an option iff ... it contains no space character"; negative-number matcher accepts "optional-sign integers and floats")
corrections.why: INCOMPLETE on two counts. (a) DIGIT CLASS: the negative-number regexes are Python `re` patterns using \d, which matches ANY Unicode Nd (decimal-digit) codepoint, not just ASCII 0-9. Arabic-Indic, Extended-Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits are all accepted as negative numbers and therefore usable as bare values after `--a`. Non-Nd numeric characters (category No, e.g. U+00BD VULGAR FRACTION ONE HALF) are not. The exact patterns are `^-\d+$` and `^-\d*\.\d+$` matched against the WHOLE token (so `--1`, `--1.5`, `-1.`, `-.`, `-1,5`, `-1_0`, `-0x10`, `-+1`, `-1e5` are all option-like => error). (b) SPACE CHECK ORDERING: the 'contains a space' test is the LAST resort in _parse_optional, applied only after exact-match, split-at-'=' exact-match, and prefix-match have all failed. A token that starts with a matching option prefix is still an option even though it contains a space. Also, only U+0020 counts - TAB, LF, CR, VT, FF and U+00A0 NBSP do NOT exempt a token.
corrections.evidence: Unicode digits accepted as values (RC=0): `--a -١٢٣ --b y --c z --d w` => LINE4 '-%D9%A1%D9%A2%D9%A3#w?value'; `--a -۵ ...` => '-%DB%B5#w?value'; `--a -１２３ ...` => '-%EF%BC%91%EF%BC%92%EF%BC%93#w?value'; `--a -٥.٥ ...` => '-%D9%A5.%D9%A5#w?value'; `--a -1٠ ...` => '-1%D9%A0#w?value'. Rejected: `--a -½ ...` => RC=2 'argument --a: expected one argument'; `--a --١ ...` => RC=2 same. Whole-token anchoring: `--a --1 ...` and `--a --1.5 ...` => RC=2 'argument --a: expected one argument' (R11's "optional-sign" wording wrongly implies these are numbers). Non-space whitespace does not exempt: `--a $'-x\ty' ...`, `--a $'-x\ny' ...`, `--a $'-x\vy' ...`, `--a $'-x\fy' ...`, `--a $'-x\ry' ...`, `--a $'-x y' ...` ALL => RC=2 'argument --a: expected one argument', whereas `--a '-x y' ...` => RC=0 LINE4 '-x%20y#w?value'. Space does not save a prefix-matching token: `-h x` (ONE argv token, with a space) => RC=0 HELP, `$'-h\t'` => RC=0 HELP, `'-h  --a'` => RC=0 HELP - R11/safe-chars predict these are positionals. But `'--a x'` (one token) => positional: `'--a x' --a p --b y --c z --d w` => RC=2 'unrecognized arguments: --a x', and `'--help x' ...` => 'unrecognized arguments: --help x'.

corrections.rule: R19 ("-help ... parsed as -h + '-elp' via the single-dash long-prefix path"; "an attached value written without '=' is re-scanned as further single-dash options")
corrections.why: MECHANISM WRONG and RULE INCOMPLETE. There is no long-prefix path: for a single-dash token argparse takes short_option_prefix = token[:2] and short_explicit_arg = token[2:], so `-help` is `-h` + explicit arg 'elp' (not '-elp'). More importantly the re-scan is an ITERATIVE loop that peels one character at a time and re-detects '=' each round, and it raises 'ignored explicit argument' in TWO cases R19 does not mention: when the remaining explicit arg becomes empty, and when it starts with '-'. Exact algorithm for a token starting with '-h' (the only short option): let sep='=' and explicit=token[3:] if the token starts with '-h=' (i.e. the part before the first '=' is exactly '-h'), else sep='' and explicit=token[2:]. Then loop: if explicit=='' -> error "ignored explicit argument ''"; if sep=='=' -> error "ignored explicit argument '<explicit>'"; if explicit[0]=='-' -> error "ignored explicit argument '<explicit>'"; otherwise queue the help action, and if explicit[0]=='h' set explicit=explicit[1:] and (if it now starts with '=') sep='=' and drop that '=', else sep='', and loop again; if explicit[0]!='h' the leftover '-'+explicit goes to extras and the queued help action fires -> exit 0.
corrections.evidence: I derived the loop and then blind-predicted 10 tokens; all 10 matched. `-hh` => RC=0 HELP. `-hh=x` => RC=2 'argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument \'x\'' (R19 predicts HELP, since the '=' is not attached to -h). `-hhh=x` => RC=2 '...ignored explicit argument \'x\''. `-hh=y=z` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument 'y=z'". `-hh=` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument ''". `-hxh=y` => RC=0 HELP (peeling stops at 'x'). `-hx=y` => RC=0 HELP. `-h-h` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument '-h'". `-hh-` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument '-'". `-hh-x` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument '-x'". `-h-` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument '-'". `-h-x` => RC=2 "...ignored explicit argument '-x'" (R19's "re-scanned as further single-dash options" wrongly predicts this is -h then leftover '-x' => HELP). Confirming the plain cases: `-hel`, `-he`, `-h1`, `-h9=3`, `-hhx`, `-hhh`, `-hx-y`, `-help` => RC=0 HELP.

corrections.why: WRONG for bytes that are not valid UTF-8. argv is decoded with surrogateescape, but sys.stderr is opened with errors='backslashreplace', so each undecodable byte is emitted to stderr as the 6-character ASCII text \\udcXX. The leftover is therefore NOT byte-for-byte verbatim.
corrections.evidence: `./test12_executable --a p --b y --c z --d w $'\xff'` => RC=2; od -c of stderr shows the last line as: 't e s t 1 2 _ e x e c u t a b l e :   e r r o r :   u n r e c o g n i z e d   a r g u m e n t s :   \\ u d c f f \\n' - i.e. the literal 6 ASCII chars '\\udcff', not the byte 0xFF. Same for an option-shaped token: `... $'--\xff'` => 'unrecognized arguments: --\\udcff'. (The verbatim-join claim IS correct for valid UTF-8: `... '' '' x` => 'unrecognized arguments:   x' with two spaces before x; `... '  ' x` => 'unrecognized arguments:     x'; `... $' --e'` => 'unrecognized arguments:  --e'.)

corrections.rule: R24 ("NON-UTF-8 BYTES ... exits 1 with a Python traceback")
corrections.why: INCOMPLETE / OVER-GENERAL in three ways. (a) It only crashes when the bad bytes land in --a, --c or --d. --b is never encoded, so bad bytes there run to completion with exit 0. (b) The crash point differs per slot, and stdout IS flushed at exit, so partial output is visible: bad --a = 0 stdout lines, bad --c = 1 line, bad --d = 2 lines. (c) The exception text is singular/plural-sensitive: one bad byte gives "can't encode character '\\udcff' in position 0", two give "can't encode characters in position 0-1". Also the PYI number in the final line is the PID and changes every run, so it must not be hard-coded. And a bad byte in a value is irrelevant if argparse errors first.

Full stderr for `--a $'\xff' --b y --c z --d w`: 'Traceback (most recent call last):' / '  File "test12.py", line 11, in <module>' / '    f = furl(args.a)  # <CJK comment>' / '        ^^^^^^^^^^^^' / '  File "furl/furl.py", line 1381, in __init__' / '  File "furl/furl.py", line 1412, in load' / '  File "furl/furl.py", line 514, in load' / '  File "furl/furl.py", line 672, in _segments_from_path' / '  File "urllib/parse.py", line 917, in quote' / "UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 0: surrogates not allowed" / "[PYI-38986:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!"; an immediately-repeated run printed '[PYI-39000:ERROR] ...'. Argparse-first: `--a $'\xff' --b` => RC=2 'argument --b: expected one argument' (no crash).

corrections.rule: R25 ("continuation lines indented to align under the prog name (25 spaces)"; "wraps for COLUMNS <= 54")
corrections.why: WRONG at narrow widths, and silent about invalid COLUMNS. argparse has a second layout mode: if len('usage: ') + len(prog) > 0.75 * (COLUMNS-2), the prog is put on a line by ITSELF and continuation lines are indented by len('usage: ') = 7 spaces, not 25. With prog='test12_executable' that is 24 > 0.75*(COLUMNS-2), i.e. COLUMNS <= 33. So: COLUMNS >= 55 -> one line; 34..54 -> prog inline, 25-space continuation indent; <= 33 -> prog alone on line 1, 7-space continuation indent. Additionally, an unset/empty/non-numeric/zero/negative COLUMNS all fall back to width 80 (no error), and COLUMNS is parsed with Python int() so surrounding whitespace is tolerated. LINES has no effect. R25 also omits that the --help option block re-lays-out: max_help_position = min(24, max((COLUMNS-2)-20, 4)), and the help text moves onto its own line when the invocation does not fit.
corrections.evidence: COLUMNS=33 => 'usage: test12_executable\\n       [-h] --a A --b B --c C\\n       --d D' (7-space indent, prog alone). COLUMNS=34 => 'usage: test12_executable [-h]\\n                         --a A\\n                         --b B\\n                         --c C\\n                         --d D' (25-space indent). COLUMNS=32 behaves like 33; COLUMNS=35 like 34. COLUMNS=20 => 'usage: test12_executable\\n       [-h] --a A\\n       --b B --c C\\n       --d D'. COLUMNS=1 and COLUMNS=5 both => prog alone then one token per line indented 7. Fallbacks to 80 (single-line usage): COLUMNS=0, COLUMNS='', COLUMNS=abc, COLUMNS=-5, COLUMNS=0x50, and unset. COLUMNS=' 40 ' => wraps exactly like COLUMNS=40. env -u COLUMNS LINES=0 => 80-column output. Help block at COLUMNS=30: 'options:\\n  -h, --help\\n        show this help\\n        message and exit\\n  --a A\\n...' (help on its own line, 8-space indent). At COLUMNS=20: '  -h, --help\\n    show this help\\n    message and\\n    exit\\n  --a A\\n...' (4-space indent, 14-col wrap).

omissions: INTERPRETER VERSION (never stated, but it pins all the above): the bundled runtime is CPython 3.12 (`strings` on the binary yields 'python3.12'; the 'options:' heading and the sep-aware 'ignored explicit argument' behaviour for `-h=x` are both 3.12-era). An implementer should target 3.12 argparse semantics specifically - e.g. 3.11 and earlier would print HELP for `-h=x` instead of erroring.

THE ARGV PRE-PASS is never mentioned by any rule and is the single most important structural fact: argparse classifies every argv token BEFORE consuming anything, stopping at the first '--'. Only 'ambiguous option' escapes from that phase, which is why it beats help and beats left-to-right consume-time errors. Any reimplementation that is purely single-pass left-to-right will mispredict `-h --=x`, `--a --=x`, and `--a p --b y --c z --d w x --=x`.

MINIMUM TOKENS THAT TRIGGER AMBIGUITY: the ONLY ambiguous tokens reachable are exactly `--` immediately followed by `=` and anything after it. Verified `--=`, `--=x`, `--=1`, `--=y`. `---a` and `----` are NOT ambiguous (they are plain unrecognized args, because the prefix '---a'/'----' matches no option name).

`-h` FOLLOWED BY WHITESPACE is an option, not a positional (see R11 correction). Concretely: the single argv tokens '-h ', '-h\t', '-h\n', '-h x', '-h  --a' ALL print help and exit 0. This directly contradicts the 'space makes a token non-option-like' folk rule.

TOKENS THAT LOOK LIKE OPTIONS BUT LEAVE REQUIRED OPTIONS UNSET produce a required-args error, never 'unrecognized arguments' - because tier 3 precedes tier 4. Observed: bare `-abc`, `-eh`, `-0h`, `-H`, `-xh`, `--HELP`, `-`, `- h`, `--A=1`, `--ab`, `--aa=1`, `---a`, `----` all give 'the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c, --d' (or the appropriate subset). You only ever see 'unrecognized arguments' when all four of --a/--b/--c/--d were successfully supplied.

AN UNKNOWN OPTIONAL CONSUMES NOTHING, so a following bare word becomes a second leftover: `-a x --a p --b y --c z --d w` => 'unrecognized arguments: -a x' (both tokens). Conversely `--unknown --a` => 'argument --a: expected one argument' (the unknown option did not swallow --a, and the consume-time error beats the leftover report).

OTHER PREFIX CHARACTERS ARE INERT: prefix_chars is '-' only, so '+a' and '/a' are ordinary positionals ('unrecognized arguments: +a' / '/a'). fromfile_prefix_chars is disabled: '@/etc/passwd' is a plain positional ('unrecognized arguments: @/etc/passwd'), no file is read.

'--' CAN NEVER BE SKIPPED TO REACH A VALUE. I explicitly probed the CPython path where _get_values strips a '--' out of a matched argument list; it does not apply here because optional actions strip '-'/'-*' from their nargs pattern. Verified: `--a -- x ...`, `--a -- --b y ...`, `--a -- -h ...`, `--a -- -x ...`, `--a -- -- x ...`, `--b y --c z --d w --a -- x` all => 'argument --a: expected one argument'; `--a p --b y --c z --d -- w` => 'argument --d: expected one argument'.

STDOUT IS FLUSHED ON THE POST-PARSE CRASH, so exit-1 runs can emit partial output. `--a p --b y --c $'\xff\xfe' --d w` writes one stdout line (the empty LINE1) before the traceback; `--d $'\xff\xfe'` writes two. R24 implies stdout is empty on exit 1, which is only true for a bad --a.
